question: Player A controls [[Mana Vortex]] and no lands at all on the battlefield. Its third ability ("When there are no lands on the battlefield, sacrifice this enchantment") triggers and goes on the stack. Player B casts an instant that counters the triggered ability. There are still no lands anywhere. Does anything else happen?
answer: Yes. Mana Vortex's third ability is a state trigger, and the game state it checks for (no lands on the battlefield) is still true after it is countered, so it immediately triggers again and goes back on the stack. A state trigger only stops re-triggering once it has resolved, been countered, or otherwise left the stack AND the triggering condition is no longer true — being countered removes it from the stack, but does not change the board, so the very next time state triggers are checked it fires again.
key_points: Mana Vortex's third ability is a state trigger, not an ordinary triggered ability
A state trigger re-checks its condition every time it leaves the stack, including by being countered
Since no lands still exist on the battlefield, the condition is still true, so it triggers again immediately
This can repeat indefinitely as long as the countering effect is available and no lands enter
common_errors: Countering the trigger permanently stops it, since the ability has already been dealt with once
The ability cannot trigger again this turn because it already triggered once
State triggers behave like ordinary triggered abilities and do not re-fire after being countered
source: hand-authored (Claude), grounded in ruling_chunks.jsonl and the pinned CR

question: Player A controls [[Greven, Predator Captain]] (base 5/5, gets +X/+0 where X is the life they've lost this turn) and has lost no life yet this turn. Player A attacks with Greven and, from its attack trigger, sacrifices a 5/6 creature: they draw 5 cards and lose 5 life. Before this trigger finishes resolving, does Player A get a chance to gain life back in response to reduce how much Greven's power increases, and does Greven check net life change or total life lost?
answer: No response is possible: the draw and the life loss both happen as part of the same triggered ability resolving, and nothing can happen in between — no player gets priority mid-resolution to do anything, including gaining life back. Greven checks total life LOST this turn, not the net change to the life total, so even if Player A's life total had also gone up by some other amount this turn, Greven's power boost is still based on the full 5 life lost from this trigger (plus any other life lost this turn), not reduced by any life gained.
key_points: The sacrifice, the draw, and the life loss all happen while one triggered ability is resolving, so no player can act in between
Nothing can be done in response to reduce or prevent the life loss once the trigger is resolving
Greven's +X/+0 is based on total life LOST this turn, not the net change in life total
Life gained this turn does not offset or reduce the life-lost total Greven checks
common_errors: A player may respond during the trigger's resolution to gain life before the life loss is applied
Greven checks the net change in life total, so gaining life back would reduce Greven's power boost
The draw and the life loss happen as two separate events a player could respond between

question: Player A controls [[Elenda, the Dusk Rose]] (1/1, gains a +1/+1 counter whenever another creature dies) and [[Angelic Renewal]]. Another of Player A's creatures dies, putting a +1/+1 counter on Elenda (now 2/2). Later that turn, Elenda herself is dealt lethal damage and dies. Player A sacrifices Angelic Renewal to return Elenda to the battlefield. How many Vampire tokens does Elenda's death trigger create, and what are Elenda's power and toughness after Angelic Renewal returns her?
answer: Elenda's death trigger creates 2 Vampire tokens, using her power as it last existed on the battlefield (2, from the one +1/+1 counter) — not her printed power. question: Player A controls [[Kumano's Pupils]] ("If a creature dealt damage by this creature this turn would die, exile it instead."). It deals combat damage to Player B's creature, but before that creature would die, Player B bounces it back to hand with an instant. Player B then recasts the same card later that turn, and it dies from an unrelated source. Is it exiled, or does it go to the graveyard normally?
answer: It goes to the graveyard normally, not exiled. Returning a permanent to hand and recasting it creates a brand-new game object with no memory of its previous existence, so the newly-cast creature was never dealt damage by Kumano's Pupils — only the old object, which no longer exists, was. Kumano's Pupils' replacement effect only applies to a creature that Kumano's Pupils itself dealt damage to this turn, and this is a different object even though it's the same card.

Kumano's Pupils' exile replacement only applies to a creature it dealt damage to this turn, tracked per object, not per card
Since the new object was never dealt damage by Kumano's Pupils, it dies and goes to the graveyard normally
common_errors: It is still exiled, because it's the same card and Kumano's Pupils already dealt it damage this turn
Bouncing and recasting a creature does not reset which effects apply to it, since it's still the same permanent
Kumano's Pupils' effect lasts until end of turn regardless of what happens to the creature in between

question: Player A controls [[Laboratory Maniac]] and casts [[Angel's Grace]] on themselves ("You can't lose the game this turn and your opponents can't win the game this turn."). Player A then empties their own library with [[Ad Nauseam]], dropping to -5 life, and later casts an instant that requires them to draw a card while their library is empty. What happens?
answer: Player A wins the game. Angel's Grace only prevents Player A from losing and prevents Player A's opponents from winning — it says nothing about Player A winning, so it does not interfere with Laboratory Maniac's replacement effect. Angel's Grace also does not stop the life loss from Ad Nauseam (it "doesn't stop loss of life from effects that say that you lose life"), so Player A's life total genuinely drops to -5, but the state-based action that would normally make them lose for having 0 or less life is suppressed this turn by Angel's Grace's "can't lose" clause. When Player A would draw from their empty library, Laboratory Maniac replaces that draw with winning the game instead, and nothing about Angel's Grace stops that.

Angel's Grace does not prevent life loss from effects that say "you lose life" (like Ad Nauseam), only changes what damage does, so Player A really does drop to -5 life
The 0-or-less-life loss (a state-based action) is what Angel's Grace's "can't lose" clause suppresses this turn, not the life total itself
Laboratory Maniac's replacement (win instead of drawing from an empty library) still applies normally, since nothing stops Player A from winning
common_errors: Angel's Grace prevents the life loss from Ad Nauseam entirely, so Player A never goes below 1 life
Since Angel's Grace says no one can win or lose this turn, Laboratory Maniac's win-the-game replacement is also prevented
Player A's life total cannot go below 1 this turn because of Angel's Grace
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135). Laboratory Maniac's own official ruling addresses the OPPOSITE direction (an OPPONENT has cast Angel's Grace) and does not itself state what happens in this self-cast scenario, which is exactly why the ruling is relevant but not sufficient alone — Angel's Grace's own asymmetric wording has to be reasoned through to reach the answer.

question: Player A controls [[Oathsworn Knight]] (0/0, enters with four +1/+1 counters; "If damage would be dealt to this creature while it has a +1/+1 counter on it, prevent that damage and remove a +1/+1 counter from it") and separately [[Polukranos, Unchained]] (0/0, enters with six +1/+1 counters; "If damage would be dealt to Polukranos while it has a +1/+1 counter on it, prevent that damage and remove that many +1/+1 counters from it"). An opponent's spell deals 4 damage to Oathsworn Knight, and a different spell deals 2 damage to Polukranos. How many +1/+1 counters does each creature have left, and what is each one's power and toughness afterward?
answer: Oathsworn Knight loses exactly ONE counter no matter how much damage was dealt — it had 4 counters, has 3 left, and is a 3/3. Polukranos loses counters EQUAL TO the amount of damage dealt — it had 6 counters, loses 2 for the 2 damage, has 4 left, and is a 4/4. The two abilities read almost identically ("prevent that damage and remove ... a +1/+1 counter" versus "remove that many +1/+1 counters") but differ in exactly the word that matters: Oathsworn Knight always removes a single counter per damage event regardless of the amount prevented, while Polukranos removes one counter per point of damage prevented.
key_points: Oathsworn Knight's ability removes exactly one counter per instance of damage prevented, regardless of how much damage that was
Polukranos, Unchained's ability removes a number of counters equal to the amount of damage that would have been dealt
Both abilities are prevention effects (615.1a): the damage never actually happens, it is replaced by the counter removal
4 damage to Oathsworn Knight (4 counters) leaves 3 counters and a 3/3; 2 damage to Polukranos (6 counters) leaves 4 counters and a 4/4
common_errors: Oathsworn Knight loses 4 counters for 4 damage, the same proportional rule as Polukranos
Polukranos loses only 1 counter regardless of the damage amount, the same flat rule as Oathsworn Knight
The damage is dealt and then counters are removed afterward as a separate cost, rather than the damage being prevented entirely
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135); Oathsworn Knight's official ruling states directly "removes only one counter ... not one counter per 1 damage prevented", and Polukranos's official ruling directly addresses damage exceeding its counter count, so both halves of the contrast are ruling_sufficient on their own card

question: Player A controls no permanents except lands and a [[Glorious Anthem]], then in one turn casts [[Enchanted Evening]] ("All permanents are enchantments in addition to their other types"), [[Opalescence]] ("Each other enchantment is a creature in addition to its other types. Each enchantment has base power and toughness each equal to its mana value"), and [[Conspiracy]] (choosing the Advisor creature type as it resolves: "Each creature is the chosen type in addition to its other types"). After all three resolve, what creature type and power/toughness does a Swamp have, and what about Enchanted Evening itself (mana value 5)?
answer: The Swamp becomes a 1/1 Advisor, and Enchanted Evening becomes a 6/6 Advisor. These three effects are mutually dependent (613.8) and must be applied in the order that lets each one's own precondition already be true: Enchanted Evening first (making every permanent, including the lands and itself, an enchantment), then Opalescence (turning every enchantment into a creature with power/toughness equal to its own mana value — 0 for a land, since a land has no mana cost, and 5 for Enchanted Evening), and only then Conspiracy (which only affects creatures, so it has nothing to work with until Opalescence has already made everything a creature). Glorious Anthem's +1/+1 (a separate, non-dependent layer 7c effect) is added on top, making the 0/0 Swamp a 1/1 and the 5/5 Enchanted Evening a 6/6.
key_points: Conspiracy only affects creatures, so it depends on Opalescence having already turned permanents into creatures
Opalescence only affects enchantments, so it depends on Enchanted Evening having already made every permanent an enchantment
The dependency chain forces the application order Enchanted Evening -> Opalescence -> Conspiracy in layer 4, regardless of the order the spells were cast or resolved

A land's mana value is 0, so Opalescence gives it base power/toughness 0/0 before Glorious Anthem's +1/+1 makes it a 1/1; Enchanted Evening's own mana value is 5, giving it a 5/5 before the anthem makes it 6/6
common_errors: The three effects apply in the order their spells were cast, so Conspiracy (cast first, in some orderings) has no creatures to affect and does nothing
Timestamp order alone determines the outcome here, the way it would for effects that do not depend on one another
A land has no power or toughness to speak of even once it becomes a creature, so Opalescence and Glorious Anthem do not apply to it
source: mined from XMage's own test suite (Section 21.135). Opalescence's official ruling walks through the general dependency methodology in detail but for a DIFFERENT three-card combination (Opalescence + Humility + Worship) -- it teaches how to reason about dependency among type/P&T-changing effects, but does not itself state the answer for Conspiracy + Opalescence + Enchanted Evening, so the ruling is relevant without being sufficient

question: Player B controls [[Emrakul, the Aeons Torn]] (protection from spells that are one or more colors). Player A has 5 Swamps untapped and [[Murderous Cut]] ("Destroy target creature", a black instant... actually sorcery? treat as castable spell) in hand. Can Player A cast Murderous Cut targeting Emrakul at all?
answer: No. Murderous Cut is a black (colored) spell, and Emrakul has protection from spells that are one or more colors, so Emrakul can't legally be the target of a colored spell at all. Since Murderous Cut has no other legal target to choose (it requires exactly one target creature), there is no legal way to cast it targeting Emrakul -- the game won't even let Player A begin casting it with Emrakul as the target, rather than letting it be cast and then fizzle later.

Murderous Cut is a black spell, so it can never legally target a permanent with protection from colored spells
Since a legal target must be chosen at the time a spell is cast, this makes casting Murderous Cut targeting Emrakul illegal from the start, not merely a spell that later fails to resolve
This is distinct from protection only preventing damage -- protection from a quality also prevents targeting by spells and abilities with that quality

Protection from colored spells only stops damage from colored sources, not targeting by colored spells

question: Player B attacks with [[Prized Unicorn]] ("All creatures able to block this creature do so"). Player A's only untapped creature is a [[Silvercoat Lion]] enchanted with [[Oppressive Rays]] ("Enchanted creature can't attack or block unless its controller pays {3}"), and Player A has no mana available. Is Player A forced to block Prized Unicorn with the Silvercoat Lion?
answer: No. A creature that can't block unless its controller pays a cost is never REQUIRED to pay that cost, even to satisfy a "must block" requirement from something like Prized Unicorn -- a player can never be forced to pay a cost in order to attack or block. Since Player A has no mana and chooses not to pay {3} anyway, the Silvercoat Lion simply isn't able to block, so it doesn't count toward Prized Unicorn's requirement at all, and Player A is not required to do anything else to satisfy it.

Player A's only creature simply doesn't block, and Prized Unicorn goes unblocked with no illegal blocking declaration

question: Player B casts [[Flame Slash]] targeting Player A's [[Atraxa, Praetors' Voice]] (4/4), then casts [[Dualcaster Mage]], whose enters-the-battlefield trigger copies Flame Slash and chooses a NEW target for the copy: Player A's [[Walking Ballista]] instead of Atraxa. The copy goes on the stack above the original Flame Slash. Before the copy resolves, Player A activates Walking Ballista's own ability twice, removing its last +1/+1 counters to ping something else, which makes Walking Ballista itself a 0/0 and it dies from a state-based action. What happens to the copy of Flame Slash, and what happens to the original?

The original Flame Slash is unaffected by any of this -- it still targets Atraxa, which is a perfectly legal target, so it resolves normally afterward and deals 4 damage, destroying Atraxa. Only the copy fizzles; the original spell's fate depends entirely on its own target, not on what happens to the copy.

When Walking Ballista leaves the battlefield before the copy resolves, the copy has no legal target and is removed from the stack doing nothing (608.2b)
The original Flame Slash still targets Atraxa the whole time and is completely unaffected by the copy's fate; it resolves normally and deals its damage

question: Player A's [[Silvercoat Lion]] (2/2, no other abilities) is enchanted with [[Armadillo Cloak]] ("Enchanted creature gets +2/+2 and has trample. Whenever enchanted creature deals damage, you gain that much life.") and attacks unblocked for 4 combat damage. Is this the same thing as the creature having lifelink, and how much life does Player A gain?
answer: Player A gains 4 life, the same total a lifelink creature would give -- but the mechanism is different, which matters if the creature ALSO has lifelink from some other source. Armadillo Cloak's life gain is not lifelink itself; it's a separate triggered ability that goes on the stack after the damage is dealt, whereas lifelink causes the life gain to happen as a result of the damage event itself, simultaneously with the damage. If the same creature had both lifelink and Armadillo Cloak, dealing damage would gain life twice for the same damage: once immediately from lifelink, and then again from Armadillo Cloak's trigger once it resolves.

If the creature had lifelink from another source as well, both would trigger independently and the life would be gained twice for the same damage instance

question: Player A taps Player B's [[Sejiri Merfolk]] with [[Take into Custody]], then casts [[Dream Leash]] ("You can't choose an untapped permanent as this spell's target as you cast it. question: Player A controls [[Meddling Mage]], which named "Well" as it entered (the right half of the fuse card [[Alive // Well]], {3}{G} // {W}). Player A then draws Alive // Well. Can Player A cast Alive alone? Cast Well alone? Cast the card fused (both halves at once)?

A split card "has" the chosen name if either of its two names matches -- so naming just one half of a fuse card is enough to also block casting it fused, even though the other half (Alive) wasn't named. question: Player A's [[Reflector Mage]] enters and bounces Player B's [[Bronze Sable]] to hand ("That creature's owner can't cast spells with the same name as that creature until your next turn"). Player A also has their OWN copy of Bronze Sable in hand. Can Player A cast their Bronze Sable this same turn?
answer: Yes. Reflector Mage's restriction only applies to the OWNER of the specific creature that was bounced -- here, Player B. It says nothing about any other player, including Player A (Reflector Mage's own controller), even though Player A holds a card with the exact same name. Player A can cast their Bronze Sable freely; only Player B is locked out of casting a Bronze Sable until Player A's next turn.

Owning a differently-sourced card with the same name doesn't matter; the restriction only cares about who OWNS the bounced object and who is trying to cast the named card
Player A, as Reflector Mage's controller, is never restricted by their own Reflector Mage
Only Player B, whose Bronze Sable was returned, is unable to cast a Bronze Sable until Player A's next turn

Since it's the same card name, all copies of Bronze Sable are frozen out of being cast by either player

question: Player A activates [[Tamiyo, Field Researcher]]'s +1 ability on turn 1, targeting [[Sylvan Advocate]] ("Until your next turn, whenever either of those creatures deals combat damage, you draw a card"). [[Sylvan Advocate]] deals combat damage on turn 1 (attacking) and again on turn 2 (blocking), drawing a card each time. On turn 3 -- Player A's next turn -- [[Sylvan Advocate]] attacks again and deals combat damage. Does this draw a third card?
answer: No. The delayed trigger set up by Tamiyo's +1 only lasts "until your next turn" -- and turn 3 IS Player A's next turn, so the effect has already ended by the time turn 3's combat happens. Only the turn 1 attack and turn 2 block (both of which happened before Player A's next turn arrived) triggered a draw; the turn 3 attack draws nothing extra from this ability.
key_points: "Until your next turn" effects expire at the start of the caster's own next turn, not at some later point within it
Since turn 3 is Player A's next turn after activating this ability on turn 1, the delayed trigger has already ended before turn 3's combat
Both combat damage instances that happened strictly before turn 3 (the turn 1 attack, the turn 2 block) did trigger a draw each
Blocking counts as "dealing combat damage" just as much as attacking does, for a trigger worded this way
common_errors: The effect lasts through all of turn 3 as well, since it doesn't expire until an action ends it
Only attacking counts as dealing combat damage for this trigger; blocking on turn 2 shouldn't have drawn a card
The effect's duration is tied to Tamiyo's own survival, so it would end early if Tamiyo died before turn 3
